title: IDIONOMO: The Intersection of the Idiographic and the Nomothetic
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: Janetos frames and republishes an essay by Georgia Gwinnett College literacy professor Kinga Varga-Dobai, arguing that the science of reading and culturally/linguistically responsive instruction are not opposing camps but mutually dependent halves of good teaching for multilingual learners. Varga-Dobai draws on her own experience learning English explicitly, sound by sound, in a Hungarian-Romanian household, to argue that systematic, explicit language instruction cannot replace cultural and linguistic responsiveness; it has to exist underneath it. She traces how her Multilingual Learner Analysis assignment forces preservice teachers to ground two required activities, one structured and one relational, in direct ethnographic observation of a single child, arguing this dual habit of mind, once built around one student, transfers to how a teacher sees every child in the room. Janetos connects Varga-Dobai's argument to Georgia's statewide literacy-coach initiative, which reported a 15% improvement in reading outcomes in high-need schools after its first year, arguing that policy investment in coaching must include cross-linguistic and cultural competence, not phonics knowledge alone.
points: Varga-Dobai's central claim, grounded in her own experience learning English explicitly as a teenager in Transylvania, is that systematic language instruction cannot replace cultural and linguistic responsiveness, it has to exist underneath it, reframing the science-of-reading versus culturally-responsive-teaching debate as a false binary.

Her Multilingual Learner Analysis assignment requires preservice teachers to pair one structured-language activity with one relational and translanguaging activity, both grounded in ethnographic observation of a single child, deliberately preventing teachers from choosing only the side of instruction they find comfortable.

The piece cites Georgia's statewide K-3 literacy-coaching mandate, roughly 1,300 coaches, and a reported 15% improvement in reading outcomes in high-need schools as evidence that coaching infrastructure needs cross-linguistic competence built in, not just phonics expertise.

Janetos's framing essay connects the argument to her own bicultural upbringing, arguing that the tension between the human core and mandated core curriculum is one every teacher of multilingual learners must learn to hold, not resolve by picking a side.
quotes: The science of reading and culturally responsive, asset-based practice are not merely compatible but mutually dependent, one without the other is incomplete. These frameworks are not in opposition, effective instruction for English learners requires both.
Systematic and explicit language instruction cannot replace cultural and linguistic responsiveness; it has to exist underneath it.

The assignment asks preservice teachers to conduct an ethnographic observation of one multilingual or multidialectal child over two to three weeks, across classroom, cafeteria, playground, and hallway, and to interview the classroom teacher, ESOL teacher, and family when possible.
The MLA is not designed for an entire class, it is designed to change how a teacher sees one child, so that they see all children differently afterward.

According to the Georgia Department of Education, universal screener data from the first year of the state's literacy coaching initiative showed a 15% improvement in student reading outcomes in participating high-need elementary schools, with the strongest gains reported in kindergarten (GaDOE, 2025).
Language knows no limits but the spirit of a second-language learner can languish when it bumps up against limitations imposed by the instructional constraints of the classroom.
